title: The Influence of Ceiling Height: The Effect of Priming on the Type of Processing That People Use
research_question: This article investigates whether, when, and how ceiling height may affect the very manner in which consumers process information and thus how they respond to products, specifically by priming freedom-related versus confinement-related concepts that, in turn, affect relational versus item-specific processing.

participants.description: Rice University students participated in three main experiments (N=30, N=100, N=34 respectively) and two ancillary studies (N=64, N=60).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Rooms with manipulated ceiling heights: high (10 feet) vs. low (8 feet) using false foam board ceilings. Colorful Chinese lanterns were used to manipulate ceiling-height salience.
Anagrams: 3 freedom-related (liberated, unlimited, emancipated), 3 confinement-related (bound, restrained, restricted), 6 filler words.
List of 10 disparate sports (sky surfing, basketball, sailing, swimming, parachuting, boxing, chess, fishing, soccer, cycling) for categorization task.
Photos of two products (coffee-table and wine rack) that were largely sleek but had some crude features, for evaluation task.
List of 36 multicategory items (6 items from 6 different categories) for free and cued recall tasks.

measures.instrument: Self-report, 3 items (free, unrestricted, open) on a 7-point scale (1=not at all, 7=very much)
Self-report, 3 items (encumbered, inhibited, confined) on a 7-point scale (1=not at all, 7=very much)

measures.construct: Total number of shared dimensions generated
measures.instrument: Count of dimensions identified by participants for sports categorization
Coded based on Linguistic Category Model (LCM) criteria (1=OID, 2=SID, 3=PSD)

measures.construct: Average number of subgroups per dimension
measures.instrument: Count of subgroups formed by participants for sports categorization
Self-report, 4 items (rough/sleek, crude/polished, coarse/refined, organic/cultivated design) on a 7-point scale
Adjusted Ratio of Clustering (ARC) scores, ranging from -1.0 to 1.0
Average number of items recalled per category when category labels were provided
Self-report, 6 items (comfortable, at ease, pleasant, agreeable, pleasant sitting, comfortable sitting)

mechanisms: Ceiling height (high vs. low) primes freedom-related vs. confinement-related concepts.
These primed concepts, in turn, stimulate predominately relational vs. item-specific processing.
Relational processing leads to integrated and abstract ideation (e.g., more shared dimensions, more abstract dimensions, fewer subgroups, emphasis on commonalities).
Item-specific processing leads to discrete and concrete ideation (e.g., fewer shared dimensions, more concrete dimensions, more subgroups, emphasis on specific features).
Perceived body state (freedom/confinement) mediates the effect of ceiling height on processing type.
implementation_implications: Retailers should consider ceiling height based on the nature of goods sold (e.g., high ceilings for abstract art, low ceilings for concrete/detail-filled art).
Higher ceilings may foster creative problem-solving and trigger memory for distally related cues.
Lower ceilings may lead to a focus on specific details, such as small print in advertisements.
Illusory higher ceilings (e.g., in airplanes) may produce similar effects on processing.
Other atmospheric variables (e.g., lighting, windows, object density, colors) that influence perceived room volume may also affect processing type.
Ceiling height effects are more likely when the ceiling height is salient (ee.g., extreme height, or visual cues drawing attention to it).

tables.description: Treatment means and standard deviations for categorization task (total number of dimensions generated, average number of subgroups per dimension, degree of abstraction of dimensions) and product evaluation task (degree of sophistication for coffee-table and wine rack) across low/high ceiling-height salience and low/high ceiling conditions.

limitations: Generalizability to more extreme ceiling heights (e.g., soaring cathedral, crawl space) is uncertain.
Generalizability to other spatial volume contexts (e.g., room width) is uncertain.
Uncertainty if alternative concepts (e.g., confinement vs. freedom) could be primed.
Uncertainty if rooms with more extreme ceiling heights prime different concepts/processes.
Uncertainty if effects occur in typical stores without explicit salience cues, though authors suggest it's likely upon store entry or with high wall displays.

mechanism_chain.description: High ceilings prime concepts of freedom and expansiveness, leading to more abstract processing and a freedom-related body state, while low ceilings prime concepts of confinement, leading to more concrete processing and a confinement-related body state.

steps.to_construct: type of cognitive processing (abstract vs. concrete)
